newsitem.title: INDIA: U.S. balloonist pleased despite falling short.
newsitem.headline: U.S. balloonist pleased despite falling short.

text.p: NONKHAR, India, Jan 20 (Reuter - U.S. adventurer Steve Fossett, haggard but cheerful, landed his balloon in northern India on on Monday after a six-day flight which shattered a world record but fell short of his goal of circling the globe.

Fossett told Reuters his "Solo Spirit" touched down at 1:05 p.m. (0735 GMT) about 150 km (95 miles) northwest of Varanasi in Nonkhar town, more than 16,000 km (10,000 miles) from his U.S. starting point.
He said that with a bigger balloon, more fuel and some luck he might have completed his failed bid to fly around the world.
"This is the first time we have seen evidence that it is possible to fly around the world via balloon. Now I didn't make it," Fossett, speaking near the landing site in a remote field, told Reuters.
"But you can see that we had some good luck in flying to the countries and with a slightly bigger balloon and better fuel supplies, it would be possible to fly around.
"I think that someone will succeed in three years. If I go again, I will have a very good chance."
Earlier on Monday, Fossett told Reuters in Delhi by telephone that he had not made up his mind whether to make another attempt at the around-the-world flight.
"It would require only a few more changes -- a bigger balloon, more fuel and a little bit more luck," he said.
Fossett took off from St Louis, Missouri on January 13, travelling eastward across the Atlantic Ocean and North Africa.

Although he fell short of his dream of being the first balloonist to fly nonstop around the world, he broke the endurance record of six days, 16 minutes for a manned balloon flight, set in 1981 by Americans Ben Abruzzo and Troy Bradley.
On Friday, Fossett broke his own record for balloon distance travel when he passed 8,747 km (5,435 miles) over Algeria. He set the earlier mark on a flight from South Korea to Canada.

Unshaven and tired after only two hours of sleep each day, Fossett said he had burned more fuel than anticipated over the Atlantic. "I didn't have enough fuel to make it all the way around the world," he said.
The 52-year-old commodities broker-turned-adventurer said he had enough fuel to carry on but did not want to fly north over the Himalayan mountains, where landing would be dangerous, or into China.
"I didn't have permission to fly over China. I am sure they wouldn't want me to come and land in their country."
Fossett said he was "uncertain" about some places in South East Asia. "So I decided that a good place to land would be in India," he said.
His balloon snagged a tree when he came down in a field. Hours later, the silvery, deflated balloon could be seen in a heap, still caught in the tree. Some dozen police stood guard.

Fossett told Reuters he would need a day or two to collect his balloon before leaving the area, probably for Delhi. U.S. officials said they hoped the Indian Air Force would fly a helicopter to the site to help Fossett move his gear out.

Before landing, Fossett had to battle stormy weather. "I came across the worst thunder cloud I've ever experienced," he said. "This is the first time that I was forced to fly in a thunderstorm. That is very dangerous."
Fossett told Reuters he was not disappointed at falling short of his goal of encircling the globe nonstop.
"It was a very good trip," he said. "I wish I could have made the biggest achievement and flown around the world. But this is also successful."
Fossett's project manager, Bo Kemper, said he believed the adventurer would make another bid for the around-the world record. "You'll see us next year," he said.
